757.title: the Rajasuya
757.hook: the kings arrive with gifts, the fire is lit, and everyone at Indraprastha is handed a job
757.howItsDone: Some retellings of the Sabha Parva hold up Krishna washing the Brahmins' feet at the Rajasuya as a picture of humility in service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, for the Rajasuya, the four brothers rode to the four directions, and at the northern gate Arjuna asked instead of forcing his way. Did you try asking at a door that wouldn't open? Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

The hall at Indraprastha is crowded. Kings have come from near and far, and none of them came empty-handed: jewels, fine cloth, horses, gold, things the poem names one after another. Priests tend the sacred fire. Food is being carried out by the basketful. And here, among the guests, are the cousins from Hastinapura, Duryodhana and his brothers, not as rivals today but as family with work to do. After all the planning, the rite itself is underway. Today the Rajasuya happens, and the question is where each person is standing.
screen: `A HALL FULL OF KINGS.` → `GIFTS BEYOND COUNTING.` → `THE COUSINS ARE HERE TOO.`

segments.voice: A rite this big needs hands, so Yudhishthira hands out jobs. In the telling, the elders Bhishma and Drona are asked to watch over everything. Kripa is put in charge of the wealth. Vidura looks after the spending. Duhshasana sees to the food. And Duryodhana is given the task of receiving the gifts the kings bring. Hold that picture for a moment. Every jewel, every horse, every bolt of silk meant for his cousin passes through his own hands first. Now look across the hall. The poem says that Krishna, the honored friend, chose a humble job of his own: washing the feet of the Brahmins who had come. The guest the whole family honors is kneeling with a basin of water. That's the Rajasuya from the inside. On paper, it's a consecration. The kings who come and bring gifts are saying, in effect, yes, we recognize you as sovereign. It's a public yes, said with gold. Yudhishthira is the center of it. But a great gathering is never only about the person at the center. It's also every person working around the edges, and what they feel while they do it. Krishna is at the edge by choice, and seems at peace there. Duryodhana is at the edge by assignment, counting someone else's wealth. The rite is the same. The view from each spot is very different. Hold onto Duryodhana at that gift table. The poem isn't finished with him. And keep an eye on the guests, too. Not every king in that hall is happy about who's being honored, and one of them is about to say so out loud.
screen: `EVERYONE IS GIVEN A JOB.` · `DURYODHANA RECEIVES THE GIFTS.` · `KRISHNA WASHES THE GUESTS' FEET.` · `ONE RITE, MANY VIEWS.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU STAND CHANGES WHAT YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind a gathering you were part of: a wedding, a holiday meal, a big day at work. Not the person at the center. Look for your own place in it. What job did you have, official or not? Did you choose it, or was it handed to you? Notice, without judging, how it felt to stand there. If you pray, you can offer that small job, and whoever you served, in your prayer. If not, simply rest with the memory. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. A royal consecration where kings bring gifts as a sign of recognition, and where everyone, from Krishna to Duryodhana, has a part to play.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, take on one small, quiet job that nobody asked you to do, and notice how it feels from the edge of the room. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Shishupala
758.hook: the rite needs someone to receive the first honor, Bhishma names Krishna, and the king of Chedi stands up
758.howItsDone: Offering arghya, water and a respectful welcome to an honored guest or to a deity, is part of traditional Hindu hospitality and worship; at the Rajasuya, the Mahabharata turns the whole scene on who receives it first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya: Duryodhana receiving the gifts, Krishna washing the guests' feet. Did you take a quiet job no one asked you to do? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND CHANGES WHAT YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Who gets served first? It sounds small until you're the host: the seating plan, the first plate, the toast. At Yudhishthira's great rite, the question has a name. The custom is to offer an honored guest the arghya, a respectful welcome of water and gifts. And one guest must receive it first, before all the others. The hall is full of kings, elders, teachers and priests. Whoever is chosen, someone else is not. Today Yudhishthira asks the question, and we meet the man who will not accept the answer.
screen: `WHO IS SERVED FIRST?` → `THE ARGHYA: THE GUEST'S WELCOME.` → `ONE CHOSEN, MANY NOT.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira turns to the eldest of the family, his grandfather Bhishma, and asks: who among these should receive the first honor? Bhishma doesn't name a king or a priest. He names Krishna. In the telling, he says that among all those gathered, Krishna shines like the sun among lights. So the youngest Pandava, Sahadeva, brings the arghya and offers it to Krishna, and Krishna accepts it. That should be the end of it. A choice made by the eldest, carried out by the host, received by the guest. But a voice rises from the crowd. It belongs to Shishupala, king of Chedi. And he is furious. Here's the first thing to know about him. He isn't a stranger. Shishupala is Krishna's cousin, the son of Krishna's father's sister. They're family, and the poem will tell us later that the bond between them runs strange and deep. Here's the second thing. Shishupala doesn't object quietly. He doesn't take Yudhishthira aside. He stands up in front of every king in the hall and makes his complaint as public as the honor was. That's what this week is about. An honor given in public, and an objection that refuses to stay small. The Rajasuya was a picture of everyone in their place. Now one man is saying, loudly, that the place is wrong. Over the next days we'll hear what he says, how the hall answers, and why Krishna waits as long as he does before he answers at all.

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind a time when someone else was honored and you weren't: a promotion, a prize, a toast, a seat at the head of the table. You don't have to judge the feeling that comes, whatever it is. Just notice where it lives in the body: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Breathe into that spot, slowly, a few times. If you pray, you can bring that moment into your prayer. If not, let the breath soften it a little. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. King of Chedi, Krishna's cousin, the man who stands up when Krishna receives the first honor at the Rajasuya.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, when someone else gets the credit, notice your first reaction, and wait one breath before you say anything. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

759.title: Shishupala
759.hook: Shishupala makes his case against Krishna's honor, and Yudhishthira goes after him with gentle words
759.howItsDone: Some Hindus who read or hear the Sabha Parva discuss this scene as a lesson in a host's duty to guests and in how to answer insult, with Yudhishthira's gentleness and Bhishma's firmness both part of the conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday we met Shishupala, king of Chedi, rising as Krishna received the first honor. When someone else got the credit, did you wait a breath? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

Shishupala has the floor, and he isn't shouting nonsense. That's what makes this scene uncomfortable. He's built an argument, point by point, and he delivers it to a hall full of kings. If you wanted to honor age, he says, there are elders here. If you wanted to honor a teacher, there's a teacher here. If you wanted to honor a king, Krishna isn't even a crowned king. So why him? It's the kind of speech that makes people in a room shift in their seats. Today we hear Shishupala's case, and watch what the host does next.
screen: `NOT NONSENSE: AN ARGUMENT.` → `NOT THE ELDEST, NOT THE TEACHER.` → `NOT EVEN A CROWNED KING.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shishupala goes through the room like a lawyer. He names the honored elders sitting right there. He names the great teacher Drona. He names Vyasa, the sage. He names Bhishma himself. Any of them, he says, had a better claim than Krishna. Then the argument turns into insult. He says the Pandavas have shamed themselves, and that Krishna has shamed himself by accepting what wasn't his. And with that he gets up to leave, and some of the kings stir with him. Now watch Yudhishthira. He's the host. It's his great day, and his choice has just been mocked in front of everyone. He doesn't send a guard. He doesn't answer insult with insult. He goes after Shishupala himself and speaks to him gently. He tells him, in effect, that this is not a fitting way to speak, that Bhishma knows what is right, and that the other kings have accepted the choice. It's a host trying to keep a guest at the table. Then Bhishma speaks, and he is far less soft. Someone who won't accept honoring Krishna, he says, doesn't need to be coaxed. So here are two answers to the same insult, side by side. The host reaches out. The elder holds firm. The poem lets both answers stand, and lets Shishupala's anger keep growing between them. And notice what Krishna is doing through all of this. Nothing. He hasn't said a word.
screen: `SHISHUPALA NAMES THE ELDERS.` · `THE ARGUMENT TURNS TO INSULT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA SPEAKS GENTLY.` · `BHISHMA HOLDS FIRM.` · then, large: `KRISHNA SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow down. Bring to mind someone whose words have stung you lately, maybe in public, maybe in a message. Picture their face for a moment. Now try Yudhishthira's way, just in your mind: not agreeing, not hitting back, just one gentle sentence you could say to them. You don't have to send it. Hold that sentence, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can name them in your prayer. If not, simply wish them steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. The king who argues against Krishna's honor, turns his argument into insult, and walks out, while the host follows him with gentle words.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, if someone's words sting, try one gentle sentence before you try a sharp one. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: Shishupala
760.hook: the angry kings gather around Shishupala, Bhishma speaks of a sleeping lion, and Bhima has to be held back
760.howItsDone: In some retellings of the Sabha Parva, Bhishma restraining Bhima, even while Shishupala mocks him, is told as a picture of an elder's self-control.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala made his case and walked out, and Yudhishthira followed him with gentle words. Did you try one gentle sentence before a sharp one? Day seven hundred sixty.

A room can turn in a few seconds. One person's anger becomes a murmur, the murmur becomes a group, and the group starts talking about a fight. That's where the Rajasuya is now. Shishupala isn't alone anymore. Other kings have gathered around him, and in the telling they begin to talk of war, of spoiling the rite before it's finished. Yudhishthira, the host, is worried, and he turns again to his grandfather. Today we watch two kinds of anger in one hall: the kind that spreads, and the kind that has to be held back.
screen: `ONE ANGER BECOMES A CROWD.` → `TALK OF WAR AT THE RITE.` → `THE HOST IS WORRIED.`

segments.voice: First, the youngest Pandava speaks up. Sahadeva, who carried the arghya to Krishna, turns to the hall and dares anyone who objects to the honor to answer him. Nobody does. Then Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what to do about the kings. Bhishma isn't troubled. He gives an image instead of a plan: these kings, he says, are like dogs barking around a sleeping lion. The lion hasn't woken up yet. It's a striking thing to say about a room full of crowned rulers. Shishupala hears it, and turns his anger on Bhishma. He mocks the old man. He tells a little fable about a bird that preaches caution while picking scraps of meat from a lion's teeth, and says that's Bhishma, all fine words and no courage. He mocks the stories told about Krishna's childhood, too. And that's when Bhima rises. The poem describes his rage as terrible to see, his eyes blazing, ready to spring at Shishupala. And Bhishma, the very man being insulted, holds him back. He calms Bhima down. So look at the hall. Shishupala's anger keeps spreading, pulling in kings, reaching for anyone nearby. Bhima's anger is just as hot, but it's caught and held by an elder who takes the insult and refuses to let it become a brawl. And Krishna, the sleeping lion in Bhishma's picture, still hasn't moved.
screen: `SAHADEVA'S DARE.` · `DOGS AROUND A SLEEPING LION.` · `SHISHUPALA MOCKS BHISHMA.` · `BHISHMA HOLDS BHIMA BACK.` · then, large: `ANGER THAT SPREADS, ANGER THAT IS HELD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the hands rest open. Bring to mind something that made you angry recently. Let yourself feel a little of it: the heat, the quickening. Now be your own Bhishma for a moment. Don't push the anger away. Just hold it, the way a hand rests on a friend's shoulder. Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. Again. If you pray, you can bring that anger into your prayer, just as it is. If not, simply keep breathing with it. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. The king whose anger spreads through the hall, who mocks Bhishma, and who stirs Bhima to a rage that Bhishma has to hold back.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, if anger rises, put a hand on it before you put a voice to it: one long breath out first. Day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: Shishupala
761.hook: Bhishma tells the hall how Shishupala was born, and why Krishna once promised his mother a hundred pardons
761.howItsDone: Some storytellers and commentators use Shishupala's birth story to explain Krishna's patience in the hall, reading his silence as the keeping of a promise to his aunt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala's anger spread through the hall, and Bhishma held Bhima back. When anger rose, did you breathe out first? Day seven hundred sixty-one.
screen: `ANGER THAT SPREADS, ANGER THAT IS HELD.`

segments.voice: The kings are muttering about war. Bhima has nearly leapt across the hall. Bhishma has been mocked to his face. And the one person all of this is about just sits there, and hasn't said a word. So Bhishma, still holding Bhima's arm, does something unexpected. He stops the argument and tells a story. It goes back to the day Shishupala was born. If you want to understand this hall, he says, in effect, you have to go back to that cradle. Today, the strange birth of Shishupala.
screen: `WHY IS KRISHNA SILENT?` → `BHISHMA TELLS A STORY.` → `BACK TO THE CRADLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Bhishma tells it. Shishupala was born in the royal house of Chedi with three eyes and four arms, and he cried out at birth with a strange, unearthly cry. His parents were frightened, and thought of giving him up. Then a voice came from no one they could see. Don't abandon him, it said. He will grow strong. His death is not yet. And it told them how to know who would end his life: the one on whose lap the child's extra arms would fall away and his third eye would vanish. So the king and queen did what any frightened parents might. They put the baby on the lap of every visitor. King after king held him. Nothing happened. Then Krishna came to visit his aunt, and the child was placed on his lap. The two extra arms fell away. The third eye sank into his forehead and was gone. Now his mother knew whose hand would one day take her son's life. And she was Krishna's father's sister. She begged him for a boon: spare my son. Krishna gave her a promise. He would pardon a hundred of Shishupala's offenses, even ones that deserved death. So that's what Krishna is doing in the hall. He isn't ignoring the insults. He's counting them. His silence is a promise to his aunt, made long ago over a cradle, being kept insult by insult. Patience, in this story, isn't the absence of anger. It's a word given, and honored, even when it costs something.
screen: `THREE EYES AND FOUR ARMS.` · `A VOICE: DON'T ABANDON HIM.` · `ON KRISHNA'S LAP, THE SIGNS FALL AWAY.` · `A MOTHER ASKS, KRISHNA PROMISES.` · then, large: `HIS SILENCE IS A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and the breath lengthen. Bring to mind a promise you've made to someone: to call, to show up, to be patient with a person who's hard to be patient with. Maybe it's one you've been keeping quietly for a long time. Let yourself see the person you made it to. Breathe in, and notice the weight of the promise. Breathe out, and notice what keeping it has asked of you. If you pray, you can hold that promise in your prayer. If not, simply honor it in silence. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. Born with three eyes and four arms, spared at his mother's plea, and pardoned by Krishna a hundred times by promise.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, keep one small promise you've been tempted to let slide, and let it cost you a little. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

762.title: Shishupala
762.hook: Shishupala challenges Krishna to fight, and Krishna finally speaks: the pardons are used up
762.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings and devotional art, the Sudarshana discus is one of Krishna's signs, and some tellers present the end of Shishupala as the moment his long patience reaches its promised limit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma told of Shishupala's birth, and Krishna's promise to his aunt: a hundred pardons. Did you keep one small promise, even at a cost? Day seven hundred sixty-two.

Bhishma's story should have cooled the room. It does the opposite. Shishupala hears that he's been spared all his life by Krishna's promise, and he's not grateful. He's insulted. He turns from Bhishma to Krishna himself and calls him out: stand up and fight me. For the first time in this whole scene, the challenge is aimed straight at the silent guest. Every king in the hall is watching. Today, after all that waiting, Krishna speaks.
screen: `THE STORY DOESN'T COOL HIM.` → `FIGHT ME.` → `THE SILENT GUEST STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer Shishupala first. He turns to the kings. In the telling, he lays out what Shishupala has done in the past: wrongs done against Krishna's own people, some of them while Krishna was far away and couldn't defend them. He reminds the hall that Shishupala is his aunt's son, and that for her sake he has borne all of this. And then he says the line the whole week has been waiting for, in effect: the hundred are full. The promise has been kept to the end. Shishupala doesn't back down. He laughs at Krishna and dares him to do his worst. So Krishna calls to mind his discus, the spinning weapon that is his in the stories, and it comes to his hand. And in front of all the kings, he strikes, and the king of Chedi falls. Sit with how this happens, because the order matters. Krishna doesn't strike at the first insult, or the tenth. He doesn't strike when Bhima wants to. He waits until his word to his aunt has been fully kept. And even then, before he acts, he explains himself to the room. The poem shows patience and judgment as two parts of the same thing. Patience isn't endless here. It has a shape and a limit, and the limit was set long ago, in love, for a frightened mother. Some readers find the ending hard. Some find it just. The poem gives us the waiting, the warning and the blow, and lets us hold all three.
screen: `KRISHNA SPEAKS TO THE KINGS.` · `FOR HIS AUNT'S SAKE, HE BORE IT.` · `THE HUNDRED ARE FULL.` · `THE DISCUS COMES TO HIS HAND.` · then, large: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle low in the belly. Bring to mind a situation where you've been patient for a long time, maybe with a person, maybe with a habit of your own. Ask yourself quietly: where is the limit here? You don't have to decide anything now. Just notice whether there's a line, and whether you know where it is. Breathe in steadiness. Breathe out the strain of waiting. If you pray, you can ask in your prayer for clarity about it. If not, rest with the question. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. The king who challenged Krishna once too often, after a hundred pardons kept for his mother's sake had run out.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, if you've been patient with something for a long time, name your limit to yourself, kindly and clearly. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

763.title: Shishupala
763.hook: a light rises from the fallen king and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira finishes his rite
763.howItsDone: In some devotional traditions, the end of Shishupala is told as a teaching that even hatred, if it fixes the mind on Krishna, can bring a person to him; other readers take a different meaning, and the Mahabharata itself does not explain the light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala used up his hundred pardons, and Krishna spoke, then acted. Did you name a limit to yourself, kindly and clearly? Day seven hundred sixty-three.
screen: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun. Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him. It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed. Today, the light, the funeral, and the end of the Rajasuya.
screen: `A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.` → `IT BOWS TO KRISHNA.` → `IT ENTERS HIM.`

segments.voice: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The poem shows it and moves on, so readers have filled the space. Some Hindus, especially in devotional traditions, read it this way: Shishupala thought about Krishna constantly, even if every thought was hatred, and that fierce, single-minded attention brought him to Krishna in the end. Others read it more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. The text doesn't settle it, and neither will we. Then the story turns practical. Yudhishthira, the host, does what a just king does after a death in his hall. He has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala, and he places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi. The fallen king's line keeps its crown. The rite is finished, the guests are honored and sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city. Now look back at the week. We started at the Rajasuya, with everyone handed a job, Krishna washing feet and Duryodhana receiving the gifts. Bhishma named Krishna for the first honor, and Shishupala stood up. He made his case, and Yudhishthira answered with gentleness. The kings grew angry, Bhishma spoke of a sleeping lion, and held Bhima back. Then the cradle, and a promise of a hundred pardons. Then the limit, and the discus. And now the light. Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE LIGHT MEAN?` · `THE FUNERAL, AND A NEW KING.` · `THE RITE IS FINISHED.` · `LOOKING BACK AT THE WEEK.` · then, large: `THE COUSIN AT THE GIFT TABLE.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let this be a resting sit after a heavy week. Bring to mind someone you've had real trouble with, someone who takes up a lot of room in your thoughts. Notice how much attention you've given them. You don't have to change how you feel. Just see the attention itself, as if it were a light you've been shining at them. Breathe in, and gather it back a little. Breathe out, and let it rest. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer for a moment. If not, simply let your attention come home. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. Krishna's cousin and fierce opponent, pardoned a hundred times, whose light rose at the end and entered Krishna.
Your line: Shishupala. Today, notice who takes up the most room in your thoughts, and where you'd rather turn that light. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

fork.setup: you're one of the kings in the hall. Shishupala has fallen, and a light rises from his body. where does it go?
fork.reveal: the poem says the light bowed to Krishna and entered him, and the kings were amazed. it shows this without explaining it.

original.note: Sanskrit tejas: radiance, brilliant energy; a light like this rises from Shishupala and enters Krishna.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story ends when Shishupala dies.
what it means: a light rises from him and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira gives him a funeral and crowns his son.
what a scholar hears: the text shows the light without explaining it, and later devotional readers took it as a teaching about the power of a mind fixed on Krishna.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (the radiance rising from Shishupala's body and entering Krishna; funeral rites; Shishupala's son installed; the Rajasuya completed)
Bhagavata Purana, Book 7, chapter 1 (the teaching that fixing the mind on the Lord, even in enmity, leads to him, with Shishupala as an example)
